title: 5. Leading KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit

epigraph.quote: Whatever we have committed, we have delivered. We started with a base of INR400 crores while we did the IPO, and today I am suggesting we will do around INR4,000 crores — that is 10x.
epigraph.author: Sanjay Lodha, Chairman & Managing Director, Netweb Q2 FY27 Earnings Call (26 October 2026)

web_blocks.html: Because Netweb's reported profit can lag its operating reality by a quarter or two, the operating KPIs matter more here than in most businesses. The metrics that lead the financials are the order book and its conversion, the AI-HPC-private-cloud mix, the operating EBITDA margin, the cash-conversion cycle, and the gating factor of all three — inventory. Management discloses each of them. That means they can be audited rather than assumed.

web_blocks.caption: Table 5.1: Netweb's Leading Operating KPI Dashboard (FY2026 through Q2 FY2027)
rows: Rising even after executing ₹2,143 crore in H1 FY27 — new order intake is outpacing billing
A conditional near-term pipeline; converts only if formally awarded
Growing; management guides a ~60% historical conversion over 18–24 months
Now the largest and fastest line; concentration and cycle sensitivity rise with it
Above the ₹14% framework; management warns not to extrapolate
84 days (FY2026, management basis); 121 days (FY2026, Screener basis)
Lengthening on the stated basis but within the guided 90–110 day band; the two bases differ because Screener does not net customer advances
Deliberate build against the order book; the single biggest working-capital risk
Improving — customers are paying faster on milestones
High retention; also evidences reliance on a concentrated base
Stable; execution speed is a competitive credential
web_blocks.takeaway: Every leading KPI is moving in the right direction except inventory and the cash-conversion cycle, which are the direct cost of that growth. The order book rising after a ₹2,143 crore billing half-year is the strongest single datum in this table.

web_blocks.html: The structural opportunity genuinely is large. India's data-centre capacity is projected to grow from roughly 1.5–1.6 GW today toward 9 GW by 2030. The IndiaAI Mission carries a ₹10,372 crore outlay and has already empanelled more than 38,000 GPUs. The National Supercomputing Mission 2.0 places explicit weight on indigenous design and manufacturing. Management has said it aims to capture more than half of the NSM 2.0 opportunity over the programme's five-year life. On top of that sits the C-DAC tender for up to 10,000 additional AI compute units under IndiaAI, where Netweb is engaged with the participating cloud service providers as an OEM supplier. The addressable backdrop is supportive. The question is not whether the market exists but whether Netweb can keep winning a profitable share of it.

web_blocks.caption: Table 5.2: Three-Year CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit — What Was Promised vs. What Was Delivered
rows: Grow at 30–40% CAGR over the next few years
Revenue grew from ₹445 crore (FY23) to ₹2,184 crore (FY26), a ~70% CAGR; H1 FY27 alone was ₹2,143 crore, up 254% YoY
Scale from roughly ₹400 crore at IPO to ₹4,000 crore revenue
FY26 delivered ₹2,184 crore; the FY27 target of ₹4,000 crore implies ~83% growth on FY26
FY26 13.0%, FY25 14%, Q2 FY27 14.9%, H1 FY27 15.1% — margins held even as scale multiplied
Keep the cash-conversion cycle near historical levels
FY26 84 days; Q2 FY27 94 days, within the guided 90–110 day band — but inventory days rose from 86 to 117
Modest capital expenditure (~₹20–25 crore) with no major expansion
FY26 capex ~₹10 crore; FY27 guided routine capex ₹20–25 crore; the constraint is working capital, not the factory
Build in India and expand manufacturing at scale
15,000 sq ft dense-GPU facility commissioned; liquid-cooled GB200/GB300 systems designed and manufactured in India
Deepen R&D and stay on the global technology cadence
Taiwan R&D subsidiary approved; Vera Rubin design work started with commercial offering planned by January 2027
web_blocks.takeaway: Across seven testable claims, management delivered five clearly, is on track on one and is in progress on the others. The one place promises are under strain is the working-capital cycle, where inventory days have risen sharply even though the headline cycle has stayed within the guided band.

web_blocks.html: There is one promise the audit cannot yet mark as delivered: new growth engines. Management has repeatedly pointed to physical AI, quantum simulators and emulators as future opportunities. But on the Q2 FY2027 call it declined to give any revenue timeline, describing them as 'initial development stage.' That is prudent, but it means the entire forward case rests on the existing AI, HPC and private-cloud lines. The Taiwan R&D subsidiary and the planned January 2027 launch of Vera Rubin-based systems are the concrete next steps. How quickly they convert into order-book additions is the KPI to watch for FY2028.

web_blocks.title: The KPI That Decides Everything: Pipeline Conversion
paragraphs: Everything in Netweb's forward case rests on one recurring assumption: a roughly 60% conversion of a growing pipeline into firm orders over 18 to 24 months. If that holds, the ₹11,152 crore pipeline supports several years of 30–40% growth and the inventory build looks prescient. If it slips — because the government's GPU procurement reprices, because hyperscalers postpone a build, or because a competitor wins a marquee tender — then the inventory becomes a liability and the order book stops rising.

Management is aware of this and has refused to lift its 30–40% guidance even when analysts suggested 50–60% growth was mathematically available. That restraint is a positive signal about management behaviour. But you should treat the 60% conversion rate as the single most important number in this dossier, because it is the number that links the demand story to the cash-flow risk.

book_paragraphs: If you were managing Netweb, what would you watch every Monday morning? Not the share price. You would watch the order book, the pipeline, the margin framework and the cash cycle, because those four numbers determine the company's fate long before they reach the income statement. Let us walk down that dashboard together, because it is where the truth about this business lives.

Start with the order book. At 30 September 2026 it stood at ₹2,629 crore of confirmed orders, plus ₹653 crore of L1 positions — contracts where Netweb is the lowest bidder but the paperwork is not signed. Behind those sits an active pipeline of ₹11,152 crore. Now notice what happened in the half-year that just ended: Netweb billed ₹2,143 crore of revenue, and the order book still rose. Ask yourself how a company can fill ₹2,143 crore of orders and end with a bigger backlog than it started. The only answer is that new orders are arriving faster than old ones are billed — and that is the single most reassuring fact in this entire dossier.

Then look at the mix. AI Systems was 43% of FY2026 revenue and 58% of Q2 FY2027 revenue, while HPC and private cloud together are now about 37%. This is the concentration question in numeric form. The AI line is where the growth is, and it is also where the competition is fiercest and the customer's decision most driven by price and delivery speed. Keep one eye on the balance between the fast line and the sticky lines.

The margin framework is the next stop, and here management deserves credit. They promised 13–14% operating EBITDA and delivered 13.0% in FY2026, 14.9% in Q2 FY2027 and 15.1% in the first half. When a company nearly doubles revenue in a year and still holds its margin, that is operating discipline, not luck. But read the fine print: management hastened to warn that the H1 figure is not a new normal, because the gross margin on a very large deal is structurally different from a small one. Believe the framework, not a single good quarter.

Now the number that should keep you awake: inventory. Look at the KPI dashboard and find the two rows moving the wrong way. Inventory days rose from 86 in March 2026 to 117 in September. The cash-conversion cycle lengthened from 84 to 94 days. Management calls the inventory build deliberate, a hedge against component lead times for a ₹2,629 crore backlog, and within a supply-constrained GPU market that is a defensible strategy. But you should be clear-eyed that it is a bet: if orders convert as expected, the inventory is a competitive weapon; if the pipeline stalls, it is a warehouse full of depreciating silicon.

Finally, the structural backdrop. The case for demand is not built on optimism alone; it rests on government policy with money behind it. India's IndiaAI Mission carries a ₹10,372 crore outlay and has already empanelled more than 38,000 GPUs. The National Supercomputing Mission 2.0 explicitly favours indigenous manufacturing, and management has said it is targeting more than half of that opportunity over five years. India's data-centre capacity is expected to grow from about 1.6 GW today toward 9 GW by 2030. This is a tailwind a company can build on — provided it keeps winning at a profit.

So how does the walk-the-talk audit come out? Look at Table 5.2 and count. Management promised 30–40% growth and delivered roughly 70%. It promised to scale from ₹400 crore to ₹4,000 crore and it is on track. It promised to hold margins and it did. It promised modest capex and it kept capex near ₹10–25 crore. Five promises delivered, one on track, and one — the working-capital cycle — where the headline is fine but the underlying inventory trend is a genuine concern. For a company of this size facing this demand, that is an unusually clean track record.

One caveat to carry with you: the new engines are still unproven. Physical AI, quantum and the Vera Rubin launch planned for January 2027 are real initiatives but carry no revenue timeline. So the forward case rests entirely on the existing lines and on one assumption — a roughly 60% pipeline conversion. If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember that number, because it is the hinge on which the entire investment case turns.

Let me close this audit with a thought about what KPIs are actually for. It is tempting to treat them as a scorecard, a way to grade management's quarter. Do not. Treat them as an early-warning system. The order book tells you whether demand is still arriving before it shows up in revenue. Inventory days tell you whether the company is buying ahead of demand or because it cannot sell. The cash-conversion cycle tells you whether growth is being financed by customers or by the balance sheet. Read together and tracked over several quarters, these four numbers will tell you that the cycle is turning long before the income statement admits it. That is their real value, and it is why this chapter exists between the segment story and the forensic audit.

book_callouts.title: Restraint as Evidence
book_callouts.text: The most telling moment of the Q2 FY2027 call was not a number but a refusal. An analyst pointed out that with a ₹10,000-crore-plus pipeline and a 60% strike rate, Netweb could plausibly grow 50–60%, and asked whether the 30–40% guidance was too conservative. Management declined to raise it: 'I cannot give a guidance on the guidance.' Founders who under-promise and over-deliver compound credibility. Hold that in mind when you weigh the more promotional claims in the sector.
